heading: Making the Android app cheap to draw
lede: Every change here is Android-only, measured on two emulators before and after, and checked pixel by pixel so the Android screens still look exactly as they did. That last part matters because the next job is making iOS match Android, which only works if Android's look stays the fixed reference.
intro_html:
What was wrong, and how each change was judged

The starting problem was not a slow screen, it was a screen that never stops. Sitting on Home, touching nothing, the budget phone drew about 10 frames a second forever and spent 646 ms of CPU per second of wall clock. On the Cars tab it was 982 ms per second — half of that phone's two cores — for a picture that looks static. The Pixel does the same work faster rather than less: 390 frames in 10 idle seconds on Cars.

Two things cause that. Something animates all the time, and each repaint costs far more than it should. Splitting one idle frame on the budget phone showed where the time actually goes:

One idle frame, budget phone, median of ~80 frames
phaseHomeCars
UI thread: animation, layout, recording the drawing2.3 ms3.6 ms
RenderThread: turning that drawing into GPU commands58 ms70 ms
Waiting for the previous frame to finish39 ms66 ms

Only 0.2–0.4 ms of each frame was spent re-recording what changed; the rest was RenderThread replaying the whole scene — 324 views of rounded clips, shadows and translucent layers. So a two-character text animation costs as much as a full-screen change, and every one of those frames competes with your taps and scrolls.

A screenshot burst during idle found the culprits: the typewriter placeholder in Home's search bar, the avatar that slides between photo and logo, and the pulsing NOW dot on Cars. Nothing else moves.

The rules each change had to obey

  • Android only. Every change is behind Platform.OS === "android", an Android-only config file, or an .android.png asset. iOS keeps its current behaviour exactly.
  • Same pixels. Twelve screens are captured on both phones before and after, then compared. Regions that animate on their own are masked out first (they differ between any two runs), and scroll positions are aligned, because a slow drag lands within a few pixels of the same offset, not on it.
  • Measured, not assumed. Three runs per build per phone. A change is only called a win when the before and after ranges don't overlap; otherwise it is reported as noise, even when the median moved.

The numbers come from dumpsys gfxinfo framestats (exact per-frame timings, not the coarse histogram buckets gfxinfo prints) and from /proc/<pid>/task/*/stat for CPU per thread, over a fixed window after each input so a screen that settles sooner isn't charged for a shorter window. Harness, device logs and raw JSON live in scripts/android-perf/.

Read the RenderThread numbers as a ratio, not as phone milliseconds. Both emulators draw through a GL translation layer to the host GPU, which makes each draw call dearer than on real phone silicon. What survives that distortion is the comparison: same device, same flow, before versus after.
